rv.q: But Kerry’s frankness also unfreezes him and Alice starts working in the restaurant to assuage her sorrow.

Part soap, part sitcom and irredeemably clumsy, this new play by April De Angelis is an absolute howler. Her target is class division, but her writing is thinly plotted and hopelessly mired in lazy assumption, reducing complex issues to crude tub-thumping and every one of its characters to a galumphing stereotype.
Granted, there is the odd good throwaway gag. But still: where are all the good plays about our crisis-ridden nation in 2022? Not at the National Theatre, that’s for sure.

As it is, it feels like it clunkily stereotypes both working-class and middle-class people to real no end beyond being confident that it’s funny enough to get away with it. And really, it’s not, despite some good individual lines, enjoyably tossed out by Ripley, who does seem to be having a ball.

But none of it seems genuine and everyone is reduced to type. Ripley does her best to make Kerry an updated version of Beverly in Mike Leigh’s Abigail’s Party, but the character is saddled with too many working-class cliches (plain speaking, foul-mouthed bawdiness) and does not have enough good jokes.
It ought to have been refreshing to see Fay Ripley – one of the mainstays of Cold Feet – return to the stage after a long absence. What a shame she has chosen such a breathtakingly clumsy piece.

April De Angelis’s comedy features an Essex-born Thatcherite who has opened a restaurant in gentrified Walthamstow. Fay Ripley gives a rip-roaring central performance and Michael Gould is perfect as a vegan Remainer attracted to brash Kerry.
